sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go syntax questions are always the first screen in a Go fresher interview — interviewers use them to confirm you have actually written Go and not just read about it. This module covers the building blocks every Go developer uses on day one: variable declarations, the type system, zero values, constants, control flow, pointers, and the blank identifier. Getting these right signals you can work in a real codebase from week one.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three rules to hold in your head:

- **Every variable has a type and a zero value.** Unlike Python (no uninitialized variables), unlike Java (instance fields get zero values but locals must be assigned), Go guarantees every variable — including local ones — starts at its zero value. There is no `null`, no `undefined`.
- **`:=` is shorthand for `var` inside a function.** Outside a function you must use `var`. Use `:=` everywhere inside functions — it is the idiomatic Go style.
- **Go has one loop keyword: `for`.** It replaces `while`, `do-while`, and `for` from Java/Python. The runtime cost is the same — it is purely a syntactic design choice to keep the language small.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Variables and short declaration** — `var x int = 5` vs `x := 5`; when `:=` cannot be used (package level, redeclaring in same scope without at least one new variable)
- **Basic types and zero values** — `bool` (false), `int` (0), `float64` (0.0), `string` (""), pointer (nil); Go has no implicit type coercion
- **Constants and iota** — `const` values are compile-time; `iota` resets to 0 in each `const` block and increments per line; used for enumerations
- **Control flow: if, for, switch** — `if` requires no parentheses; `for` replaces `while`; `switch` does not fall through by default; `for range` iterates slices, maps, strings, channels
- **Arrays basics** — fixed-length, value type (`[3]int{1,2,3}`); rarely used directly — prefer slices
- **Pointers basics** — `&x` gives address, `*p` dereferences; Go pointers cannot do arithmetic (safer than C); `new(T)` allocates zeroed T and returns `*T`
- **Blank identifier** — `_` discards values; used to ignore error returns (not recommended) or loop indices

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **`:=` outside a function** — This is a compile error. Package-level variables must use `var`. Freshers who only practiced in `main()` get caught here.
- **Zero value of a pointer is `nil`, not zero** — Dereferencing a nil pointer panics at runtime. The fix: always check `if p != nil` before dereferencing an unfamiliar pointer.
- **`switch` does not fall through** — unlike C or Java, Go `switch` cases break automatically. To fall through, use the `fallthrough` keyword explicitly. Interviewers love this gotcha.
- **Arrays are value types** — assigning an array copies it entirely. This surprises Python/Java developers who expect reference semantics. The correct answer: use slices, which are reference-like descriptors.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In Go, every variable has a statically known type and a zero value — there is no such thing as an uninitialized variable. Inside a function I use `:=` for short declaration, which infers the type from the right-hand side; at package level I use `var`. Go's single `for` keyword replaces all loop constructs, and `switch` does not fall through by default — those two design decisions keep the language small and readable."*
